mcqs.question: A team only adds latency-by-endpoint instrumentation to the specific endpoint that just caused an incident. What's the limitation of this reactive approach?
options: It fully solves observability, since the broken endpoint is now covered
Every other endpoint remains just as uninstrumented and blind as before, so the next incident on a different endpoint hits the same gap
It's actually worse than having no instrumentation at all
Reactive instrumentation is always more accurate than proactive instrumentation
mcqs.explanation: Reactive, incident-driven instrumentation only closes the specific gap that incident exposed, leaving every other component just as blind — the next incident on a different endpoint hits the same lack of visibility. It's not worse than nothing, and there's no inherent accuracy advantage to adding it reactively versus proactively.

mcqs.question: A load balancer routes traffic to instances based only on a liveness check, not a readiness check. What production problem does this cause?
options: The load balancer will never route to any instance
An instance that's alive but still warming up (e.g. loading a cache) receives real traffic before it's actually ready to serve it correctly, causing errors
Liveness and readiness checks are the same thing, so this causes no issue
The instance will be restarted unnecessarily on every deploy
mcqs.explanation: Liveness only confirms the process hasn't deadlocked; it says nothing about whether the instance has finished warming up and can correctly serve requests. Routing on liveness alone can send traffic to a not-yet-ready instance, producing real errors. The two checks answer different questions, and this scenario doesn't involve restarts.

mcqs.question: A new service ships with only custom, hand-picked metrics and none of the golden signals. What's missing?
options: Latency, traffic, errors, and saturation — the baseline set that covers most "is this service healthy" questions without needing to anticipate every specific failure mode
Nothing, as long as the custom metrics are detailed enough
A dedicated dashboard-building team
A rewrite of the service in a different language
mcqs.explanation: Golden signals — latency, traffic, errors, saturation — form the baseline that covers general health without requiring you to predict every specific way the service could fail; custom metrics alone, however detailed, tend to be reactive and gap-prone by comparison. Neither a dashboard team nor a rewrite addresses the actual missing instrumentation.

mcqs.question: A team is deciding how much observability to build into a brand-new service before shipping it. What's the recommended default?
options: Skip instrumentation entirely until the first incident forces the issue
Build exhaustive custom instrumentation for every conceivable failure mode before shipping anything
Ship golden signals plus a health endpoint as the non-negotiable floor, then add deeper instrumentation incrementally as real failure modes emerge
Wait until the service has been in production for six months before adding any instrumentation
mcqs.explanation: Golden signals plus a health endpoint is the practical floor — cheap to build, and covers most general health questions — with deeper, custom instrumentation added incrementally as actual failure patterns show up. Skipping instrumentation entirely or waiting months both leave the service blind exactly when it matters, and over-building everything up front tends to waste effort on unused instrumentation.

mcqs.question: In a system design interview, a candidate draws a detailed architecture diagram but mentions monitoring only briefly at the very end, if time allows. How does this typically read to the interviewer?
options: As a strong signal of prioritization skill
As neutral — observability isn't expected to come up in system design interviews
As a sign that observability was never actually part of the design thinking, regardless of how correct the rest of the architecture is
As evidence the candidate is following the interview format correctly
mcqs.explanation: Treating observability as an afterthought signals it wasn't part of the actual design process, which experienced interviewers read as a gap in production experience — independent of how sound the rest of the architecture is. It's not a prioritization win, isn't neutral in a system-design context, and isn't simply "correct format."
